title: Harrison Smith, Jelly Roll Morton's estate and Fletcher Henderson's poverty
summary: Johnston describes publisher Harrison Smith's litigation over Jelly Roll Morton's estate. Gil returns to Henderson dying in poverty.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Harrison Smith who was one of the early, well a negro, a music publisher, and which promoter, he went into business in 1926, quite early for negro business, Handy was in before that, but nevertheless, still early. And right now he's in litigation with Jelly Roll Morton's estate.

And Jelly Roll owed him a great deal from some of his songs. Now this is his story, of course. Took some of his songs that he himself had written and sold them because he needed the money for something and Jelly Roll had a name at that time, you see.
And anyway, it was all the result is very complicated.
Oh you mean Jelly Roll took his songs and sold them?
And anyway they had disagreements and.....
I've seen that happen a lot of times. I mean.......

I think Jelly Roll's car was repossessed or something and Smith was helping him out. Well anyway, it turned out that Jelly Roll went out to California with still New York licence plates on his car and he died while he was out there. And someone out there laid claim to the estate. And of course it was probated out there and people were totally unaware of what was going on.

So this man got, who owns so many rights to Jelly Roll's music is all tied up in litigation now trying to get something back from people who have absolutely no right to the estate at all. And they made out the will and left Jelly Roll's wife a dollar for instance. (LAUGHTER).
I can't understand it. Some day I'm going to ask Willard Alexander that too. This was a booker, trying to get me some work and he used to be Benny Goodman's man, the booker.
I'm going to ask him some time, how come?
